doc.title: Don Menza and Sam Noto interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, January 28, 1997

title: Kenton's remark about Basie 'all they do is swing'
summary: Noto's story of the 1955 band going to hear Basie at Birdland and Kenton's comment on the bus.

story.theme_name: Playing with Count Basie: joining, leading, leaving
story.community_name: Playing with Count Basie: the band, its feel and its people

blocks.x: I’ll tell you a story about the swinging thing. This was in the ‘55 band, that was about the swingingest band that I ever was on with Kenton, I was with them for seven years. It was Al Porcino, and you know, really some swing players. We were in New York, we had a night off, so Al Porcino, who’s got that voice, I don’t know if you know who he is, but anyway, he said, “Count Basie’s band is down at Birdland. I think everyone should go down and listen to Count Basie.” So we all did, but not because he said it, but we wanted to hear him anyway you know. And Basie’s band was really hot at that time. And Stan Kenton was in the audience too. I saw him across the room and the whole thing in Birdland. So the next day we get on the bus now, we’re leaving New York and we’re going somewhere, I don’t know, to the next gig, and Al says, “Stan! I saw you at Birdland last night. How did you like Count Basie’s band?” And Stan says, “Oh it was great,” he says, “but all they do is swing.” And the whole bus cracked up, man, the whole bus cracked up. But we know what he meant, that wasn’t, that was just the way he thinks about it. He thinks more like in structures and you know—
You know, yeah. But the way he said it.
And it’s funny, he used to put down some classical music and operas and everything, and yet his concept had to do with that, had to do with that staging, that kind of presentation. His jazz concept.
